content:
Pick up a glass of water and watch the straw look broken at the surface. That bend is refraction, and it opens week seventeen, aptly named Light Work, a full tenth of the physics paper in one go.
Chemistry shifts into purification and characterisation, the lab methods for separating and identifying organic compounds. Mathematics introduces differential equations, where rates of change themselves become the puzzle. Skim yesterday’s notes on integrals so the new equations do not feel like a foreign language.
It is a big week, so do not slip on the first day. Attempt today’s three questions.
description: JEE daily challenge for 23 November 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 23 November 2026

content:
Wicked is a musical about a person who decides the old rules do not have to apply to them, and Sunday is a good day to take a leaf out of that book. Two weeks of integrals can make anyone doubt their calculus, but doubt is not data.
Look back over EM waves, the biomolecule structures and the integrals you handled this week. Notice which ones felt like a showstopper and which still need rehearsal.
Close the week the way a curtain call does. Three questions, then take a bow.
description: JEE daily challenge for 22 November 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 22 November 2026

content:
Zootopia 2 returns to a city where every species has its own habitat and its own rules, and integration is a similar zoo. Substitution, parts, partial fractions and definite properties each live in a different enclosure and need a different handler.
Today you also revisit electromagnetic waves, where a few formulas cover most questions, and biomolecules, where reading the structure correctly is the whole game. Pick the technique first, then write the first line, and the rest becomes bookkeeping.
You do not need to be a zookeeper to pass the paper. Pick up three questions and prove it.
description: JEE daily challenge for 21 November 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 21 November 2026

content:
Kantara stages its biggest moments in near darkness, with a few flames and shadows telling the whole story. Visible light is just as narrow a slice: a sliver of the spectrum, between ultraviolet and infrared, that our eyes happen to catch.
Think of the rest of the spectrum as the forest beyond the torchlight, and revise which waves are used for imaging, cooking and communication. Chemistry’s carbohydrates and integration complete a three-part set for Friday. Remember the order from radio to gamma, and the rest follows.
Step into the dark and find the answers. Attempt the three questions today.
description: JEE daily challenge for 20 November 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 20 November 2026

content:
The router blinking beside your study desk pushes out microwaves all day, and your phone is always listening for the same wave. That is the real-world version of the electromagnetic spectrum, and exam questions love asking which wave does what.
Chemistry’s biomolecules deliver proteins, enzymes and vitamins, a topic that rewards students who read the NCERT lines slowly. Integration lets you finish the set with some honest algebra. Keep a one line note for each wave type and its everyday use; those lines save time later.
If your Wi-Fi can send millions of packets a second, you can send three answers. Go attempt today’s questions.
description: JEE daily challenge for 19 November 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 19 November 2026

content:
India lifting the Women’s World Cup showed what a team can do when preparation and nerve arrive on the same day. Doing well in the physics paper looks similar, and one dependable scoring chapter is Electromagnetic Waves, which leans on a handful of relations between speed, wavelength and frequency.
Pair it with biomolecules, where memorising structures properly pays back immediately, and integration, where a clean setup beats a clever trick. Fewer formulas, cleaner setups, and a calm head are what separate a fifty from a duck.
Midweek is where the season is decided. Pick up your bat and attempt the three questions.
description: JEE daily challenge for 18 November 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 18 November 2026

content:
Stranger Things taught a generation to treat a flickering light bulb as a signal from another dimension. The real flicker is in frequency: electromagnetic waves span radio at one end to gamma at the other, and the ordering of that spectrum is a classic JEE memory test.
Biomolecules join in with glucose structures and amino acids that need careful drawing, while integration keeps asking you to pick the right technique before you start writing. Writing the spectrum order from memory once is worth more than reading it five times.
A strong Tuesday beats a hopeful Friday. Take today’s three questions and keep the week moving.
description: JEE daily challenge for 17 November 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 17 November 2026

content:
Your phone is receiving a wave right now that has no colour, no sound and no weight, and yet it carries every reel you scroll. Electromagnetic waves are the quiet backbone of modern life, and they headline this week’s Wave Hello.
Alongside, chemistry moves into biomolecules, the carbohydrates, proteins and vitamins that your own body is built from. Mathematics keeps going deeper into integral calculus, because one week was clearly never going to be enough. Treat it as a hello to three new ideas at once, and expect the first few minutes to feel unfamiliar.
Monday is a launch day. Start the week by attempting today’s three questions.
description: JEE daily challenge for 16 November 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 16 November 2026

content:
Laapataa Ladies built its charm around two people ending up in the wrong place and the wrong hands, a mix-up that took the whole film to straighten out. A lot of JEE errors are the same kind of mix-up: the right formula applied in the wrong direction.
This week gave you induction and the sign that flips when direction changes, amines whose reactivity depends on who is nearby, and integrals that care about limits. Check which of those mix-ups still catches you.
Treat today as a lost and found desk. Three questions, find what is still missing.
description: JEE daily challenge for 15 November 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 15 November 2026

content:
Children’s Day is when schools hand out sweets and cancel class, and every JEE aspirant quietly wonders if the holiday applies to them. It does not, but a short window of calm is still a good time to take on a hard set.
Electromagnetic induction asks how much voltage a changing flux creates, amines ask how much the nitrogen is willing to share, and integration asks how much area sits under a curve. All three are quantity questions in different clothes.
Remember being unafraid of tough puzzles? Go attempt today’s three questions with that same energy.
description: JEE daily challenge for 14 November 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 14 November 2026

content:
Today is Friday the thirteenth, the one date on which people suddenly become very careful about walking under ladders. Physics has a calmer relationship with bad luck: a changing flux induces a voltage whether the date is cursed or not.
So keep your head on straight and use that composure on amines, where basic strength depends on solvent and substituents, and on integration, where a missed constant of integration has cost many students real marks in real exams.
Luck does not appear in the marking scheme. Attempt today’s three questions and let preparation do the work.
description: JEE daily challenge for 13 November 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 13 November 2026

content:
An F1 pit stop lasts under three seconds and every second is a sum of tiny gestures from twenty people. That is integration in spirit: lots of small contributions adding up to a total you can actually measure.
Today’s physics brings the electromagnetic induction you met earlier in the week, including how a spinning coil generates its own opposing voltage. Chemistry’s amines and nitrogen compounds ask for precision on the same scale, one lone pair at a time.
A good pit crew drills before the race, not during it. Your three questions are the drill.
description: JEE daily challenge for 12 November 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 12 November 2026

content:
Tap pay on UPI and the whole thing takes two seconds, but the phone that did it was charged by an AC adapter turning wall power into steady DC. Alternating current is just electromagnetic induction on repeat, flux changing again and again.
Chemistry adds nitrogen compounds, where amines behave as bases and diazonium salts open doors to a dozen other products. Mathematics asks you to integrate, which is a fancy way of finding total area when change keeps shifting.
Three questions are ready. Solve them while the payment confirmation tone is still fresh in your head.
description: JEE daily challenge for 11 November 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 11 November 2026

content:
In Squid Game the rules punish anyone who moves when they should not, and the universe has an equivalent: Lenz’s law says an induced current always flows in the direction that opposes the change that made it. Nature is basically the red light.

Chemistry looks at both ends of a period — ionisation enthalpy on the left, electron gain enthalpy on the right — and maths adds up an A.P. with a condition attached.
Three questions. Beat the static friction; the kinetic part is easier.
description: JEE daily challenge for 18 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 18 August 2026

content:
Chandu Champion is a film about one stubborn idea: a champion is just a person who refused to break routine. Week 3 of the mission begins today and it is named Forces of Habit — Newton’s laws, periodic trends, arithmetic progressions. Rules that repeat, rewards that compound.
Physics opens with the classic incline experiment: how much faster does a block slide down when friction disappears? Chemistry ranks first ionisation enthalpies across Na, Mg, Cl and Ar — a trend with a trap in it — and maths starts a two-week friendship with arithmetic progressions.
Week 3, day 1. Three questions. Champions train on Mondays.
description: JEE daily challenge for 17 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 17 August 2026

content:
Two batters clear the ropes at the same spot: one flat and vicious, one a towering loft. Same range, wildly different hang time. Physics has a name for this pair — complementary angles of projection — and today it asks exactly how their times of flight compare.
It is Sunday, the final day of Motion & Atoms. Chemistry works out the radius of the helium ion’s first excited state against hydrogen’s first orbit, and maths pins down when both roots of a quadratic go negative.
If projectiles or the Bohr model still feel shaky, revisit them today — Week 3 brings Newton’s laws and a new set of rules. Three questions to close the week; finish not out.
description: JEE daily challenge for 16 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 16 August 2026

content:
Every August 15 morning, somewhere in India a tricolour balloon bunch slips loose and rises steadily into the sky. Today’s physics is exactly that picture: a balloon climbing at 10 m/s, a stone released at 75 m. The stone does not fall straight away — it inherits the balloon’s upward velocity first. Freedom, but with initial conditions.
Independence Day, Week 2, day 6. Chemistry quizzes you on quantum numbers — the constitution every electron in the universe must obey — and maths finds when a quadratic has no real roots at all.
The holiday is real; so is the streak. Three questions between the flag and the biryani.
description: JEE daily challenge for 15 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 15 August 2026

content:
Nobody: absolutely nobody: JEE examiners: two cars are moving at 100 km/h and 80 km/h in the same direction. You have watched this exact scene from a bus window a hundred times — the slow overtake that seems to take forever. That forever has a formula, and it is called relative velocity.
Day 5 of Motion & Atoms. Alongside the cars, chemistry lists statements about hydrogen’s orbital energies and dares you to spot the wrong ones, and maths asks how many complex numbers can satisfy two conditions at once.
Tomorrow is a holiday; today is not. Three questions — overtake the version of you from yesterday.
description: JEE daily challenge for 14 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 14 August 2026

content:
Stree 2 packed theatres because everyone loves a spectre. Chemistry has its own version — the spectrum — and unlike the movie kind, this one shows up only when strict rules are obeyed. A spectral line appears for a transition only if the selection rules allow it.
That is today’s chemistry: judging whether a given transition will actually produce a line. Physics differentiates a velocity expression to catch the acceleration at a point, and maths hunts the integral values of a parameter that keep both roots of a quadratic positive. Week 2, day 4 — the atoms half of Motion & Atoms is peaking.
Three questions tonight. The spectrum only appears to those who look.
description: JEE daily challenge for 13 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 13 August 2026

content:
Hostel rule number one: the bottom bunk goes first. Nobody wants to climb; everybody settles for the lowest comfortable spot. Electrons operate exactly the same way — they fill the lowest-energy orbital available and only move higher when forced to.
Today’s chemistry asks which hydrogen orbitals have the lowest energy, and there is a twist most students miss about hydrogen specifically. Physics, midway through Motion & Atoms, accelerates two masses and compares the distances they cover in the same time, while maths keeps you honest with another complex numbers workout.
Week 2, day 3. Three questions — claim your bottom bunk before someone else does.
description: JEE daily challenge for 12 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 12 August 2026

content:
Watch an Olympic diver leave the 10-metre platform: for one heartbeat they hang there, then gravity runs the show, faster and faster until the water. Every frame of that fall is governed by the three kinematics equations you are living with this week.
Today’s physics drops a ball from 18 m and asks at what height its speed crosses a particular value — a diver question in disguise. Chemistry, day 2 of Motion & Atoms, compares the Balmer and Brackett series of the hydrogen spectrum, and maths counts solutions of a quadratic that depends on a natural number.
Three questions. Entry with minimal splash, please.
description: JEE daily challenge for 11 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 11 August 2026

content:
Pushpa 2 did not become a monster hit by standing still — every frame of that film is momentum and swagger in motion. Fitting, because Week 2 of Mission JEE 2027 starts today and it is called Motion & Atoms: learn to describe how things move before you explain why they move.
Kinematics enters your life with a projectile whose x and y coordinates are handed to you as functions of time — find the launch angle. Chemistry goes subatomic with the Bohr model’s energy levels, and maths leaves the real line behind for complex numbers.
New week, new chapters, same rule: three questions today. Nobody flexes until the streak says seven days.
description: JEE daily challenge for 10 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 10 August 2026

content:
A Mumbai local at 8:47 am waits for nobody, but notice how commuters sort themselves: everyone bound for the same station drifts toward the same door. Same destination, same group — that is today’s maths relation, which clubs ordered pairs together by their second coordinate.
It is Sunday, the last day of Week 1. Physics closes Ground Zero with dimensions hiding inside a position equation, and chemistry makes you rank the actual masses of everyday substances — water, acid, carbon, salt.
If units or moles still make you nervous, today is the day to revisit them, because Week 2 brings Kinematics and the atom. Three questions first — end Week 1 on a full platform.
description: JEE daily challenge for 9 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 9 August 2026

content:
Kalki 2898 AD built a whole future — flying machines, a fortress city, tech nobody explains. Here is the boring truth behind every sci-fi machine: if its parts carry fractional errors of 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5, the whole build’s error stacks up frighteningly fast. Precision is the least glamorous superpower.
That stacking is literally today’s physics question: independent errors combining through a formula. Chemistry drops marble into acid — calcium carbonate meeting HCl — and asks for the gas bill, while maths makes you picture two regions in the plane and find where they overlap.
Day 6 of Ground Zero. Three questions — build your 2898 with tighter tolerances.
description: JEE daily challenge for 8 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 8 August 2026

content:
When Swiggy batches three orders to one delivery partner, it is grouping by neighbourhood: same area, same trip. Group things by a rule that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, and mathematicians call it an equivalence relation. Your dinner has been running set theory for years.
Today, day 5 of Ground Zero, maths asks you to count the equivalence relations on a small set — small set, surprisingly sneaky counting. Physics wants the maximum percentage error in a wire’s density from its measured mass and radius, and chemistry runs a Dumas-method nitrogen estimation, a classic mole workout.
Three questions before dinner arrives. Thirty minutes, or it is on your conscience.
description: JEE daily challenge for 7 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 7 August 2026

content:
Oppenheimer spends half its runtime on people scribbling symbols on blackboards, and audiences worldwide sat through three hours of it. Those symbols work because physicists agree on one thing before anything else: dimensions. Get those wrong and the blackboard is just doodling.
Day 4 of Ground Zero. Today you find what the ratio of vacuum permeability to permittivity is dimensionally equal to — a genuinely famous JEE trap. Chemistry asks how many mL of concentrated nitric acid carry 30 g of the pure acid, and maths tests whether the greatest integer function can shake you.
Three questions. Now you are become the solver of dimension problems.
description: JEE daily challenge for 6 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 6 August 2026

content:
Umpire’s call is the most argued-about phrase in cricket, and it exists because every measurement has an error margin. Ball-tracking is brilliant, but even it must admit: within this much, we cannot be sure. DRS is basically error analysis with better graphics.
Day 3 of Ground Zero runs on the same idea. Physics gives you a system’s energy with measurement errors in the quantities and asks how the uncertainty propagates. Chemistry turns steam and hot iron into a mole-ratio problem, and maths checks whether you actually know what a given function is doing.
Three questions today. Take the review — you cannot leave this one to the third umpire.
description: JEE daily challenge for 5 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 5 August 2026

content:
Every UPI payment you make lands in exactly one account. Never two, never none. Congratulations — you already understand one-one functions; you have just never been paid marks for it. Today’s maths question asks you to count one-one functions between sets, which is UPI logic with factorials.
Meanwhile physics hands you L, C and R and asks what dimensional formula their combination gives — Week 1, day 2, and Ground Zero is already testing whether you speak the language of dimensions. Chemistry removes molecules from a sample and asks what mass you started with: pure mole-concept accounting.
Three questions, one sitting. Scan the QR code of your own discipline and pay up.
description: JEE daily challenge for 4 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 4 August 2026

content:
In 12th Fail, the whole story turns on one word: restart. No shortcuts, no plan B, just back to page one and grind. Today is your restart. Mission JEE 2027 starts now, and Week 1 is called Ground Zero for a reason.
This week is foundations: Units and Measurements in physics, the mole concept in chemistry, and sets in maths. Nobody brags about these chapters, but every mark you score in 2027 will quietly stand on them. Today you match fundamental constants to their dimensions, work out how much magnesium buys you 220 mL of hydrogen, and untangle a solution set.
Three questions. Fifteen minutes. Day 1 of the mission — show up.
description: JEE daily challenge for 3 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 3 August 2026

content:
Pushpa 2 has a man hauling logs worth more than cars. Here is the physics nobody in the film mentions: a log rolling down a slope is not just spinning and not just sliding - it is doing both at once. Combined translational and rotational motion, today’s physics headache.
Meanwhile the smuggling business runs on a truth chemistry students know: things split. Dissolve salt in water and one particle becomes two - the van’t Hoff factor is chemistry admitting its particle count went off script. And every consignment that may or may not get caught? That is a probability distribution with real stakes.
Pushpa never backs down from a job. Your job today is three questions - take it.
description: JEE daily challenge for 2 August 2026: one Physics, one Chemistry and one Mathematics question from past JEE papers, with worked solutions.
title: Daily Challenge — 2 August 2026

content:
In 12th Fail, Manoj does not crack the exam with one heroic moment. He restarts, and he counts everything - pages read, hours slept, rupees left. Small measurements, taken honestly, every single day.
That is exactly today’s mood. A screw gauge exists because a ruler is too arrogant for the small stuff - it reads down to a hundredth of a millimetre. The mole exists because atoms are too many for honest counting, so chemists bundle them, 6.022 x 10^23 at a time. And when you add small terms one by one and watch the total behave, that is summation of series.
Small things, counted right, become ranks. Three questions today - restart, and attempt all three.

title: Daily Challenge — 1 August 2026

content:
What is JEE Notes? JEE Notes is a free study platform for students preparing for the Joint Entrance Examination (JEE Main and Advanced). It covers the full syllabus — 20 Physics chapters, 20 Chemistry chapters, and 14 Mathematics chapters — with concept notes, formula sheets, solved previous-year questions, full-length mock tests, and a daily challenge.
Everything on this site is free, with no signup, no login, and no paywall. You can read, print, or copy any page as Markdown.
Who runs it JEE Notes is operated by HappyChases Media Works (OPC) Private Limited, an Indian company. We are an independent study resource — not affiliated with the NTA, any IIT, or any coaching institute (see the full disclaimer).
How the content is made — and checked We believe you should know exactly how the material you study was produced:
Concept notes are written against the current NTA syllabus, structured for exam preparation: core concepts from first principles, worked formulas with their conditions of validity, memory aids, common-mistake warnings, and practice problems at three difficulty levels. Previous-year questions and mock tests use real JEE Main papers. Every MCQ answer is validated against the official NTA final answer key. Worked solutions are drafted with the help of AI tools and are being progressively reviewed for step-by-step correctness. Pages whose solutions are still in the review queue say so. We would rather tell you this plainly than pretend otherwise — for a definitive answer, the NTA key is always the authority, and we mark our solutions as ours. Found an error? Mistakes in exam-prep material cost marks, so we treat error reports as the highest-priority input. If a solution step, formula, or answer looks wrong:
Leave a comment on the page (every topic page has a comment section), or Reach us through the contact details in our terms — error reports are read and actioned ahead of everything else. Corrections ship in the next daily site build.
Why trust a free site? Fair question. Our answer: check us. Every solution shows its working so you can verify each step against your own; every answer can be checked against the official NTA key; and our terms, privacy policy, and disclaimer name the company and grievance contact behind the site. We keep the site free because the material costs us little to host — and a student in a small town with no coaching budget deserves the same quality of revision material as anyone else.
description: Who runs JEE Notes, how the study material is made and checked, and how to reach us — a free, no-signup JEE Main & Advanced preparation resource.
